blocks.explanation:
An infinite A.G.P. with \(|r| < 1\): the terms shrink, so the sum is a fixed number. Same multiply-by-\(r\)-and-subtract method, but there is no last term, and the middle becomes an infinite G.P. with sum \(\frac{\text{first term}}{1 - r}\).
A.P. part \(1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots\); G.P. part \(1, \frac12, \frac14, \ldots\), \(r = \frac12\).
Plan: write \(S\) and \(\frac12 S\) shifted, subtract, sum the infinite G.P., then check with \(S_\infty\) of 6.8.2.
steps:
Given: \(1 + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{5}{4} + \frac{7}{8} + \cdots\); \(a = 1, d = 2, b = 1, r = \frac{1}{2}\)
To find: the sum to infinity \(S\).
Method: Since \(|r| = \frac12 < 1\) the sum exists; multiply by \(r\), shift, subtract.

Write \(S\) and \(\frac12 S\)
\[S = 1 + \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{5}{4} + \dfrac{7}{8} + \cdots\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{5}{8} + \cdots\]
Why: Multiplying by \(\frac12\) puts one more 2 in each bottom; shift one place so equal bottoms line up.

Subtract
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = 1 + \dfrac{2}{2} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{2}{8} + \cdots\]
\[= 1 + \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \cdots\right)\]
Why: \(S - \frac12 S = \frac12 S\); each pair leaves \(d = 2\) on top, e.g. \(\frac{3 - 1}{2} = \frac{2}{2}\). The first term 1 stays; there is no last term.

Sum the infinite G.P.
\[1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = 2\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = 1 + 2 = 3\]
\[S = 6\]
Why: Infinite G.P. sum \(\frac{a}{1 - r}\) with first term 1, \(r = \frac12\); then multiply by 2.

Check with the formula
\[S_\infty = \dfrac{ab}{1 - r} + \dfrac{dbr}{(1 - r)^{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{2}} + \dfrac{2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{4}}\]
\[= 2 + 4 = 6 \;\checkmark\]
Why: The 6.8.2 formula with \(a = 1, d = 2, b = 1, r = \frac12\) gives the same sum.

blocks.explanation:
An infinite A.G.P. with \(|r| < 1\): the terms shrink, so the sum is a fixed number. Same multiply-by-\(r\)-and-subtract method, but there is no last term, and the middle becomes an infinite G.P. with sum \(\frac{\text{first term}}{1 - r}\).
A.P. part \(2, 5, 8, 11, \ldots\); G.P. part with \(r = \frac13\).
Plan: write \(S\) and \(\frac13 S\) shifted, subtract, sum the infinite G.P., check with the formula.
steps:
Given: \(2 + \frac{5}{3} + \frac{8}{9} + \cdots\); \(a = 2, d = 3, b = 1, r = \frac{1}{3}\)
To find: the sum to infinity \(S\).
Method: \(|r| = \frac13 < 1\); multiply by \(r\), shift, subtract.

Write \(S\) and \(\frac13 S\)
\[S = 2 + \dfrac{5}{3} + \dfrac{8}{9} + \dfrac{11}{27} + \cdots\]
\[\tfrac{1}{3}S = \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{5}{9} + \dfrac{8}{27} + \cdots\]
Why: Multiplying by \(\frac13\) puts one more 3 in each bottom; shift one place.

Subtract
\[\tfrac{2}{3}S = 2 + \dfrac{3}{3} + \dfrac{3}{9} + \dfrac{3}{27} + \cdots\]
\[= 2 + \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{9} + \cdots\right)\]
Why: \(S - \frac13 S = \frac23 S\); each pair leaves \(d = 3\) on top, e.g. \(\frac{5 - 2}{3} = \frac{3}{3}\); the first term 2 stays.

Sum the infinite G.P.
\[1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{9} + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{2}\]
\[\tfrac{2}{3}S = 2 + \tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{7}{2}\]
\[S = \tfrac{7}{2} \cdot \tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{21}{4}\]
Why: \(\frac{a}{1 - r}\) with first term 1 and \(r = \frac13\); then multiply by \(\frac32\).

Check with the formula
\[S_\infty = \dfrac{ab}{1 - r} + \dfrac{dbr}{(1 - r)^{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{2}{\frac{2}{3}} + \dfrac{3 \cdot \frac{1}{3}}{\frac{4}{9}}\]
\[= 3 + \dfrac{9}{4} = \dfrac{21}{4} \;\checkmark\]
Why: With \(a = 2, d = 3, b = 1, r = \frac13\) the formula agrees.
